title: Inscribed Rectangle Surface Transformation
full_prompt:
Write a complete ManimGL script using the 3b1b/manimlib framework that visualizes the relationship between a 2D loop and its corresponding 3D midpoint-distance surface (used in the topological proof of the inscribed rectangle theorem). 

Your scene, named `ChangeTheSurface`, should perform the following sequence:
1. Initialize a 3D scene with a 2D loop (e.g., an ellipse or a smooth deformed loop) lying on the xy-plane.
2. Show two points, $A(u)$ and $B(v)$, moving along the loop. Draw a line segment connecting them, highlight their midpoint on the xy-plane, and project a vertical line up to a height $z$ equal to the distance between $A$ and $B$.
3. Generate the full 3D parametric surface defined by: $S(u, v) = (\text{midpoint}_x(u,v), \text{midpoint}_y(u,v), \text{distance}(u,v))$ for $u \le v$ (or the half-parametric version to avoid double-counting, creating a Mobius-like ribbon/surface).
4. Rotate the camera to a 3D perspective to clearly show the surface's height representing chord length.
5. Smoothly morph the 2D loop into a different shape (e.g., from an ellipse to a clover-like loop) and animate the 3D surface dynamically morphing to match the new loop's geometry using an updater or a custom transition.

Ensure you use ManimGL's 3D rendering capabilities, including proper surface shading, custom dot glows, and smooth camera rotations.

common_failure_modes.pattern: Using Manim Community Surface syntax instead of ManimGL ParametricSurface
common_failure_modes.note: ManimGL's ParametricSurface expects a function returning a 3D array/list and uses u_range/v_range differently than Manim Community.

common_failure_modes.pattern: Failure to dynamically update the 3D surface when the 2D loop morphs
common_failure_modes.note: The surface must be bound to the loop's shape via an updater or reconstructed smoothly during the transition.

common_failure_modes.pattern: Incorrect domain mapping for the half-surface
common_failure_modes.note: Mapping the full square [0,1]x[0,1] results in self-intersection and double-covering. The half-parametric function helper must be used correctly.
